facts.claim: "Drink a Beer" was written by Jim Beavers and Chris Stapleton and recorded by Luke Bryan.
Chris Stapleton, who co-wrote the song, sang harmony/background vocals on Bryan's recording.
Beavers arrived at the writing session with the whole chorus already written. Stapleton says he suggested making the song darker and about someone who had died.
Beavers said he and Stapleton recorded only a simple guitar-and-vocal demo, with Stapleton singing in one take.
Bryan has said that when someone emailed him the song and he listened to it, it "tore me to pieces".
Bryan lost his brother Chris in 1997 and his sister Kelly in 2007, which is why the song hit home for him.
Bryan has described the song as "the coolest sad song ever".
It was released in November 2013 as the third single from Crash My Party and reached No. 1 on Billboard Country Airplay in February 2014.
Bryan has said that before this song he was known as the party guy, and that it showed another depth of his artistry.

research.lineage: The song sits in mainstream Nashville country, a Nashville-written ballad of grief that contrasts with the upbeat party singles Bryan was known for, such as "Rain Is a Good Thing" and "Country Girl (Shake It For Me)".

draft:
The person in **Drink A Beer** gets the worst phone call of their life and does the only thing that makes sense: "So I just hung up the phone." No speech, no prayer, no casserole. Just a walk that ends at the water and a decision not to go home yet. That's the whole plot, and the song never asks for more.

Jim Beavers and Chris Stapleton wrote it, and the story of how is worth knowing. Beavers came into the session with the chorus already finished: sit on the pier, watch the sun go down, drink a beer. Stapleton says he pushed to make it darker, to make it about someone who had died. That instinct changes everything. The same small ritual that could have been a lazy-evening song becomes what a person does when the alternative is falling apart. The beer isn't celebration or even escape. It's something to hold while the news sinks in.

The verses are honest about how badly grief fits the comforts people offer. The narrator reaches for the standard line, "the good Lord knows the reasons why," then hangs a weak "I guess" on it and admits "I can't make it all make sense." Faith and confusion sit next to each other and neither one wins. The narrator doesn't reject the greater plan, just can't feel it right now, and the song lets that stay unsettled.

The real turn comes in the last section. After "So long my friend," the chorus comes back, but now it's attached to "all the times that we used to." The pier was their spot. Every chorus before that was the narrator sitting alone in a place built for two, and only at the end do you learn it. Saying goodbye and keeping the habit turn out to be the same act.

For Luke Bryan, the song hit somewhere real. He lost his brother Chris in 1997 and his sister Kelly in 2007, and he said that when the song came to him by email, it "tore me to pieces." The Beavers and Stapleton demo was just guitar and voice, with Stapleton singing it in one take. Jeff Stevens produced Bryan's version, and Stapleton stayed on for harmony vocals, so one of the writers is still present under the finished record.

It's a Nashville grief ballad that came from an artist known for "Country Girl (Shake It For Me)," and Bryan said it showed a depth people hadn't heard from the party guy. He called it "the coolest sad song ever." It went to No. 1 on country radio anyway, maybe because nearly everyone has a version of that pier.

The song sticks because it understands that when words fail, you go back to the place and repeat the small thing you used to share, and that counts as mourning too.
